title: trataka
hook: a curtain is pulled back in a temple, and a crowd leans forward to see and be seen

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka as dharana you can see: the mind tied to one place. Which task did you give a post to, and how many times did you walk back? Day one thousand thirty.

Evening at a temple. A small crowd stands packed in front of a closed curtain, shoes left at the door, hands holding flowers and little plates of sweets. Bells. Then the curtain is drawn aside, the lamp is lifted, and there is the image of the deity, dressed and garlanded, eyes wide. Nobody in the crowd looks away. Some fold their hands. A grandfather lifts a small boy higher so he can see. This is darshan. And it raises a question about trataka: when the thing you gaze at is not a mark on a wall, what changes?
screen: `THE CURTAIN IS DRAWN ASIDE.` → `A CROWD LEANS IN TO SEE.` → `WHAT IF THE MARK IS SACRED?`

segments.voice: Darshan means seeing, or a sight. In temple worship it names the moment of beholding the deity in the image, the murti. People speak of going to the temple for darshan, the way someone might say they're going to visit family. And in the way some devotees describe it, darshan isn't only looking. The deity is also looking back. The worshipper sees, and is seen. That changes the gaze. In trataka on a candle, the eyes do the work, and the flame doesn't care. In darshan the eyes are meeting someone. The Bhagavad Gita has a scene about the limits of that meeting. In chapter eleven, Arjuna asks Krishna to show him his supreme form. And Krishna answers, in paraphrase: you cannot see me with these eyes of yours. I give you a divine eye. Behold my power. Then the vision comes, vast and blazing, more than Arjuna can hold. So the Gita says plainly that ordinary eyes aren't enough for that kind of seeing. Something has to be given. Here's where this meets the practice. Some who practice trataka choose a sacred image as their point: a picture of a deity, a symbol like Om, the face of a teacher. The method stays the same. A steady gaze, a gentle return, the image held behind closed eyes. But the gaze is now also a kind of attention offered to someone. Teachers differ on this. Some keep trataka strictly to a flame or a dot, to keep it simple. Others welcome a sacred image. Patanjali, as we saw yesterday, leaves the choice open.
screen: `DARSHAN: SEEING, AND BEING SEEN.` · `THE GAZE MEETS SOMEONE.` · `ARJUNA IS GIVEN A DIVINE EYE.` · `A SACRED IMAGE AS THE POINT.` · then, large: `THE MARK LOOKS BACK.`

segments.voice: Choose your point. If you keep a sacred image, a deity, a symbol, a photo of a teacher, set it at eye level. If not, a flame or a simple mark is just as good. Rest the eyes on it softly, blinking when you need to. If it's an image that matters to you, let the gaze feel like a greeting rather than a stare. When the eyes tire, close them and hold what stays. Then look again. The bell holds the time.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, its neighbor darshan, where the gaze rests on a sacred image, and the worshipper sees and is seen.
Your line: seeing and being seen. Today, when you greet someone, give them one full, unhurried look before you speak, the way you'd look at something that matters. Day one thousand thirty.

howItsDone: Temple-goers speak of going for darshan, the sight of the deity in the murti, which in some temples comes at set times when the curtain is opened and a lamp is offered; some practitioners of trataka use a sacred image as their point of gaze.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: darshana, seeing, a sight. In temple worship, beholding the deity in the murti.

trapdoor: what you thought: darshan is a glance at a statue.
what it means: it's beholding the deity, and, as devotees describe it, being beheld.
